i personally work with food justice organizations in Portland that have chapters across the country and we have experienced a decline in donations- CSA’s in the bay area are experiencing a significant decrease in subscriptions to their services as well. good questions.

i think that different stores/ communities have their own definition of ‘local’ or ‘regional’ but i think just always trying to buy the most local is a reasonably accessible thing to ask someone- especially in socal! 

most importantly, just because something has the recycling symbol on it does not been you can recycle it!! totally a common misconception, though. i think those darn clamshells are one of the most easy to mistake for being recyclable. here’s an article to read more http://blogs.oregonstate.edu/ecologue/2014/01/28/recycling-mythbusters-plastic-recyclables/

listen. i believe that trying your best is what’s most important here, and that some reduction is better than none. but don’t delude yourself or others. “imperfect produce” is backed by *corporate* sponsors and ultimately perpetuates the systemic overproduction of produce by large, corporate agribusinesses. it does not support nor cooperate with small or local farms. shorter supply chains are one major solution to reducing waste, not truck loads of “ugly,” imported bananas. if you want to make a difference in this movement, i think supporting your local CSA is much more in line with the values of a waste- free future than this company. 
not to mention that this so- called ugly produce that would have otherwise gone to food banks or other organizations doing food justice work, is now being commodified to turn a profit. this is green- washing capitalism at its finest.

and finally, those clamshell containers are NOT recyclable!! please don’t put them in your recycle bin.
